extracted.intended_audience: Voters/citizens considering ratification and readers interested in constitutional design and executive powers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and standards for structuring the national executive (term length, re-eligibility, compensation, veto, appointments, military command, judicial separation, etc.), argued in the Federalist Papers to guide adoption of the proposed U.S. Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The unity of the executive is one of the best distinguishing features of a constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single executive (versus a plural council) promotes accountability and decisive action. Multiple executives or councils can become instruments of faction, cloak faults, and increase expense by requiring members to reside at the seat of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration in Office (term length) as prerequisite of executive energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer duration in office increases the probability of firmness and independence in the executive's exercise of constitutional powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short tenure produces feebleness and irresolution because officeholders with precarious tenure are less willing to risk unpleasing but necessary actions. A term of years (discussed specifically as four years) is not perfect but materially contributes to firmness while not endangering liberty; too short a term weakens independence and yields slavish pliancy to immediate popular or legislative humors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-eligibility of the Executive (no permanent exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing the chief magistrate to be re-elected promotes stability and preserves the advantages of experience and established administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding re-eligibility (temporary or perpetual) undermines incentives to good behavior, tempts corruption or usurpation as incumbents seek to extract maximum gain before forced exit, deprives the nation of accumulated experience especially in emergencies, causes mutability of measures, and prevents the public from continuing effective administrations by popular choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate Provision for Support (fixed compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President should receive stated compensation that cannot be increased or diminished during the term, and should not receive other emoluments from the Union or any State during that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixing compensation for the term prevents the legislature from coercing or corrupting the executive via pay (reducing him 'by famine' or tempting by largess). It secures material independence by eliminating pecuniary leverage and disallows other emoluments that could influence conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified Negative (veto) on Legislative Acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive is given a qualified negative: the power to return bills with objections, preventing them from becoming law unless subsequently ratified by two-thirds of each legislative house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The veto serves as both a defense for the Executive against legislative encroachment and as a check to prevent hasty, faction-driven, or improper laws. A qualified (rather than absolute) negative encourages cautious use, makes its exercise less offensive, and ties the executive's objection to substantial legislative support for override (two-thirds), increasing its practical efficacy while reducing abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent Powers and Means to Administer (appointment & supervision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters of administration (foreign negotiations, finance plans, disbursement of public money, army/navy arrangement, directions of war) should be managed by persons who are assistants or deputies of the chief magistrate, deriving offices from his appointment and subject to his superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to appoint and supervise subordinates connects the duration and authority of the chief magistrate with stability of administration. Without this control, new incumbents will likely reverse predecessors' measures, causing mutability and ruinous instability in governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of Branches / Separation of Powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The partition of government must render each branch independent of the others; separation is meaningless if one is dependent on another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being subordinate to the laws differs from being dependent on the legislature. Dependence allows the legislative body to absorb other branches; republican assemblies especially may attempt to exercise imperious control. Constitutional design must provide each branch arms (powers and protections) to defend against encroachment and preserve balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto as a Safeguard Against Legislative Haste and Faction
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive negative helps guard the community against faction, precipitancy, or impulses unfriendly to the public good that may influence a legislative majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated examination by diverse parts of government reduces the risk of collective error. The veto is particularly useful to prevent laws passed through haste or by contagion of passion; while it may defeat some good laws, that injury is outweighed by the prevention of many bad ones and greater legislative stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness of the Judiciary (avoid combining judges with executive functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should be kept distinct from executive avocations and not be placed in regular association with the Executive (e.g., as members of an executive council) to avoid bias or dangerous combinations between executive and judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associating judges with executive revisionary capacities could improperly bias them as interpreters of the law, induce them to embark in political views, corrupt judicial independence, and cement an unsafe alliance between executive and judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of Administration (avoid mutability of measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution should promote administrative stability so that measures and policies are not subject to disgraceful and ruinous mutability due to frequent changes in the chief executive or his subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate term length, re-eligibility, and control over subordinate appointments all serve to maintain a steady system of administration; prohibitions on continuing effective officeholders (exclusion) or frequent purges encourage harmful turnover of measures and loss of institutional memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of Military and Naval Forces (centralized military leadership)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to be commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States and of the militia when called into actual service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direction of war and military operations peculiarly demand qualities best exercised by a single hand; concentrating military command in the executive enables effective, decisive leadership during hostilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning Power of the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive is vested with the pardoning power (as indicated by section header: 'The Command of the Military and Naval Forces, and the Pardoning Power of the Executive').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While detailed argumentation is not present in this chunk, the pardoning power is presented as one of the executive's prerogatives tied to its proper constitution and functions.
